head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: True if `a` occurs in `s` starting at index `i`
Checking a pattern at a position
Sorted lists of all start positions of `a` and `b` in `s`
Index of the first `b`-position that is at least `i − k`
Binary search in a sorted list
That position is also within `i + k`, so some `b` lies in the window `[i − k, i + k]`
Collect the answers in order (`pa` is already sorted)

p: `s = "isawsquirrelnearmysquirrelhouseohmy"`, `a = "my"`, `b = "squirrel"`, `k = 15`. Then `pa = [16, 33]` and `pb = [4, 18]`.
Both are beautiful: `[16, 33]`.

blocks.h: Why only check the first position in range?
p: If any `b`-position lies in `[i − k, i + k]`, then the smallest position that is `≥ i − k` is also in that window (it can only be smaller or equal). So testing just that one position is enough.

bullets: Time: O(n · (|a| + |b|) + |pa| log |pb|) for the scans and the binary searches.
Space: O(n) for the position lists.

3006.takeaway: Find all positions of a and b, and for each a-position binary-search the nearest b-position at or after i − k.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: How many times each value occurs
The subset is determined by counts
The value 1 squares to itself, so any odd number of 1s works as the pattern `1,1,...,1`; if the count is even, drop one
A special case in the pattern
`y = x; while cnt.get(y, 0) >= 2: length += 2; y *= y`
Climb the chain `x, x², x⁴, ...`: while at least two copies exist, the value can sit on both sides of the palindrome
If one copy of the next value `y` exists it becomes the peak (`+1`); otherwise the last pair must give up one element to be the peak (`−1`)
Keep the longest pattern over all starting values

p: The best subset is `{2, 4, 2}`, so the answer is `3`.

blocks.h: Why `−1` when the next value is missing?
p: Each loop step counted 2 for a value that has two copies. If the next square `y` is absent, the pattern still needs a single peak, and the only candidate is the last value counted. It can appear only once in the middle instead of twice, so the total is reduced by 1.

bullets: Time: O(n · log log max), since each chain squares the value and ends fast.

3020.takeaway: For each starting value follow x, x², x⁴, ... while pairs exist and end with a single peak; handle 1 separately.

head: Code
Meaning

rows: Maximum operations if every operation must have this score
Fix the one thing that is common and solve
Best number of operations on the remaining subarray `nums[l..r]`
Interval DP (dynamic programming over ranges) with memoisation
Fewer than two elements left, no operation possible
Delete the first two, the last two, or the first and last, each only if the sum equals `score`
The first operation must be one of the three moves, so the score is one of three values
The score is fixed by the first operation

p: `nums = [3,2,1,2,3,4]`, `score = 5` (the first two sum to 5).
Three operations in total, so the result is `3`.

Whatever the first operation is, it removes one of the three pairs at the ends of the original array. Its sum then fixes the score of all later operations, so trying those three sums covers every possible plan.

bullets: Time: O(n^2) states per score, three scores.

3040.takeaway: Fix the score from the first move (three options), then memoised interval DP counts the most operations that keep that sum.

The AND (bitwise AND) of the array can only keep bits common to all
We need the `(n−1)`-th number after `x` in the sequence of valid numbers; its index written in binary decides the free bits
This bit position is free: `x` has 0 here, so the elements can use it
Put the next bit of `k` into this free position
Spreading the bits of a number into the gaps of another
Move to the next bit of `k` only after using a free position

p: The valid sequence is `4, 5, 6`, and the last element is `6`.

blocks.h: Why does this give the minimum?
p: All valid elements are `x` plus extra bits in the free positions. Listing them in increasing order is the same as counting upward in binary using only the free positions as digits. The `(n − 1)`-th such number is `x` with the bits of `n − 1` placed into the free positions, which is exactly what the loop builds. The first element is `x` itself, so the AND cannot contain more bits than `x`, and every element contains all of `x`'s bits, so the AND is exactly `x`.

3133.takeaway: The last element is x with the binary digits of n − 1 poured into the zero bits of x.

The sum of two numbers is odd exactly when one is even and one is odd
Every neighbouring pair must satisfy it (true for a single element)

p: Both pairs differ in parity, so the result is `True`. For `[4,3,1,6]` the pair `(3, 1)` sums to 4, so `False`.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: The last day already covered by the merged meetings so far
`if s > end: busy += e - s + 1; end = e`
A new meeting starts after the frontier: all its days are new
`elif e > end: busy += e - end; end = e`
The meeting overlaps the frontier but extends it: only the extra days are new

p: Free days = `10 − 8 = 2` (days 4 and 8).

blocks.h: Why only count the new days?
p: Overlapping meetings share days, and counting each meeting fully would count those days twice. Tracking the furthest covered day (`end`) means each day is added exactly once.

bullets: Time: O(m log m) for sorting.

3169.takeaway: Sort the meetings, count each busy day once with a running end, and subtract from the total days.

Generating all strings with a rule
A complete string has been built
A `0` can be appended only at the start or after a `1`, otherwise two zeros would be adjacent
Return the strings in order (the recursion visits `1` before `0`)

p: `n = 3`. The recursion tree (a string can only be extended with `0` if it is empty or ends in `1`):

blocks.h: Why is it enough to check the last character?
p: Two adjacent zeros always include the last character of the prefix and the new one. The rest of the string was already valid, so checking the end is sufficient.

bullets: Time: O(n · F), where F (about 1.6^n, the Fibonacci numbers) is the count of valid strings.
Space: O(n) recursion depth plus the output.

3211.takeaway: Build strings by backtracking, allowing a 0 only when the string is empty or ends with 1.

p: A substring with `z` zeros needs at least `z²` ones, so its length is at least `z² + z`, which cannot exceed `n`. Therefore the loop `while z * z <= n` visits only the possible zero counts, giving O(n √n) overall.

3234.takeaway: For each start, count dominant substrings by the number of zeros z (at most about √n), using next-zero jumps to count valid end positions as a range.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Converting a letter to an index
Parity of the sum: squares of the same colour have sums of the same parity

p: `"a1"` has column 0 and row 1, so parity 1. `"c3"` has column 2 and row 3, so parity 1. They match.
`a1` and `c3` have the same colour (`True`); `a1` and `h3` do not (`False`).

blocks.h: Why does parity give the colour?
p: Moving one square sideways or up changes the column or the row by 1, which flips the parity of their sum, and neighbouring squares have different colours on a chessboard.

3274.takeaway: Two squares have the same colour exactly when column + row has the same parity for both.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: How many times the value `v` occurs in `nums`
`c = sum(cnt[k] for k in range(g, m + 1, g))`
Pairs among them: every such pair has a gcd (greatest common divisor) that is a multiple of `g`
`- sum(exact[k] for k in range(2 * g, ...))`
Remove pairs whose gcd is a larger multiple of `g`, leaving pairs with gcd exactly `g`
Running total of `exact[1..g]`: how many sorted gcd values are `≤ g`
The smallest `g` for which `pref[g] > q`, i.e. the gcd at sorted index `q`

p: `nums = [2,3,4]`, `m = 4`. Going from `g = 4` down to `1`:
Cumulative counts for `g = 1..4` are `[2,3,3,3]`. For queries `0, 2, 2`: `bisect_right(pref, 0) + 1 = 1`, and `bisect_right(pref, 2) + 1 = 2`. The result is `[1,2,2]`.

blocks.h: Why not compute all pairs' gcds?
p: There are about `n²/2` pairs, which is far too many for `n = 10^5`. Counting by value uses only the maximum value `m`, with a harmonic-sum amount of work.

bullets: Time: O(m log m + q log m).

3312.takeaway: Count pairs by gcd value using multiples and inclusion–exclusion, then answer each query with a binary search on the cumulative counts.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Count of each value in the current window
A value's "strength": higher count wins and, on ties, the larger value wins; tuples compare in exactly that order
Sorted list of the `x` strongest pairs (weakest first)
Elements that contribute to the x-sum
Sorted list of all the other pairs (strongest last)
Current x-sum: for each pair in `top`, count times value
Take a pair out, put one in, then fill `top` up to `x` pairs and swap while `rest`'s best beats `top`'s worst
Keeping the invariant "top holds the strongest x"
Remove the old pair of `v`, change its count, add the new pair, rebalance
One element enters or leaves the window

p: The answers are `[6,10,12]`.

Only the `x` strongest pairs contribute to the sum. When a count changes, at most the boundary between `top` and `rest` moves, so a few swaps restore the invariant. This avoids re-sorting all values for every window.

bullets: Time: roughly O(n · d), where `d` is the number of distinct values in a window: list searches, inserts and removals are linear in the list size. A balanced tree or heap with lazy deletion would give O(n log n).

3321.takeaway: Maintain the top-x (count, value) pairs and their sum while the window slides, rebalancing two sorted lists after each element enters or leaves.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Number of ways to have chosen two disjoint subsequences whose gcds are currently `a` and `b` (gcd (greatest common divisor) `0` means "still empty")
The state is the gcd of each subsequence
Put the number into the first subsequence
Put the number into the second subsequence
Both are non-empty and have equal gcd

p: `nums = [1,1]`. Each number can be skipped or sent to one of the two subsequences.
Only `(1,1)` has both non-empty with equal gcd: 2 ways (the first `1` in the first subsequence and the second in the other, or the reverse). That matches the expected answer for two equal ones.

blocks.h: Why gcd 0 for an empty subsequence?
p: `gcd(0, x) = x`, so the first element added to an empty subsequence sets its gcd to that element, and later numbers combine as usual. No separate "is it empty" flag is needed.

bullets: Time: O(n · S), where S is the number of (a, b) states, bounded by about 200² (values up to 200).

3336.takeaway: DP (dynamic programming) over pairs of gcds for the two subsequences, where each number is skipped or added to one of them.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Sorted so the elements within `k` of a target form a contiguous block
Candidate target values: each number and the points `x − k` and `x + k`
The best target is either an existing value or at a boundary of some number's reach
`near = bisect_right(nums, t + k) - bisect_left(nums, t - k)`
How many numbers lie in `[t − k, t + k]`, i.e. can become `t` with one operation
Counting a range in a sorted list
Numbers already equal to `t` need no operation
Free ones plus as many convertible ones as the operations allow

p: `nums = [5,11,20,20]`, `k = 5`, `numOperations = 1`.
The best is `2`.

blocks.h: Why test `x − k` and `x + k` as well?
p: The number of elements within reach of `t` only changes when `t − k` or `t + k` passes an element, i.e. at `t = x + k` or `t = x − k`. Between such points it stays constant. The part `same` only matters at existing values. So all useful targets are among these candidates.

3347.takeaway: Try each candidate target, count the elements within k via binary search, and add the free equal ones plus as many conversions as allowed.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Sieve of Eratosthenes: which numbers are prime
The start and the target must not be prime
Cheapest known cost to reach each number, counting the starting value
Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm; the "weight" is the value of the number reached
Always expand the cheapest unfinished number
Decrease or increase one digit by 1 (if it stays in `0..9`)
Move only to non-prime numbers, and only if it is cheaper
The first time the target is popped, its cost is minimal

p: `n = 10`, `m = 12`. Going 10 → 11 is not allowed (11 is prime). A cheapest valid route is 10 → 20 → 21 → 22 → 12, and the cost is the sum of every value, including the first.
The answer is `85`.

blocks.h: Why Dijkstra and not plain BFS (Breadth-First Search)?
p: Each move has a different cost (the value of the number you land on), so the shortest path in the number of moves is not the cheapest. Dijkstra handles non-negative edge weights and always pops the cheapest number first.

bullets: Time: O(V log V) with V up to 10^d numbers and 2d edges each, plus the sieve.

3377.takeaway: Treat numbers as graph nodes, move by changing one digit by 1 to a non-prime number, and run Dijkstra with the landed value as the edge cost.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Number of paths from `(0,0)` to `(i,j)` whose XOR (exclusive OR) is `x`
Counting paths with a running aggregate
Cell values are below 16, so every XOR is below 16
A small value range makes the extra dimension cheap
The path consisting of the first cell
XOR with the current cell undoes it: a path ending here with XOR `x` came from a path with XOR `x ^ cell`
A path arrives from above or from the left

p: `grid = [[2,1,5],[7,10,0],[12,6,4]]`, `k = 11`. The first row, where only one path exists to each cell:
So `dp[0][2][6] = 1`. Continuing the table for all cells, `dp[2][2][11] = 3`, which is the result.

blocks.h: Why recover the previous XOR with `x ^ cell`?
p: If the path up to the previous cell had XOR `y` and the current cell is `c`, then the new XOR is `y ^ c = x`, which means `y = x ^ c`. So the number of ways to end with XOR `x` equals the number of ways to end the previous cell with XOR `x ^ c`.

3393.takeaway: DP (dynamic programming) over cells and the XOR value so far (16 possible values), where a path with XOR x here came from one with XOR x ^ cell.

Meaning

rows: Interval indices sorted by start (ties by index), and the sorted starts
Binary search for "the next interval that starts after this one ends"
Best result using at most `k` more intervals, looking only at `order[p:]`; the result is a pair `(total weight, tuple of indices)`
DP (dynamic programming) with memoisation that also tracks the chosen indices
Take it and continue with the first interval whose start is strictly greater than `r` (touching endpoints overlap)
The chosen set as a sorted tuple
`cand[0] > best[0] or (cand[0] == best[0] and cand[1] < best[1])`
Prefer a higher weight and, on a tie, the lexicographically smaller index list

p: `intervals = [[1,3,2],[4,5,2],[1,5,5],[6,9,3],[6,7,1],[8,9,1]]`. Some compatible choices (at most 4 intervals):
The best weight is 8, reached by `[2,3]`.

blocks.h: Why store the tuple with the score?
p: The question asks for the lexicographically smallest list among the best ones. Comparing tuples of sorted indices when the weights tie gives exactly that, and storing it in the DP value avoids reconstructing it afterwards.

bullets: Time: about O(n log n): 4 · n states, each with a binary search and a tiny sort.

3414.takeaway: Memoised DP over positions in start order and the remaining number of intervals, with ties broken by the lexicographically smaller index tuple.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Minimum cost so far when the current outer pair of houses has colours `a` (left) and `b` (right)
Process houses from both ends inward
The two mirror houses must differ
Move one pair inward at a time
`min(v for (p, q), v in dp.items() if p != a and q != b)`
The previous pair `(p, q)` must differ from the new colours on its own side, because those houses are neighbours
Best total over all colourings of the innermost pair

p: `n = 4`, `cost = [[3,5,7],[6,2,9],[4,8,1],[7,3,5]]`. The pairs are houses `(0,3)` and `(1,2)`. One cheapest colouring is `0, 1, 2, 1` for houses 0 to 3.
The colouring has no equal neighbours, and the mirror pairs (houses 0 and 3, and 1 and 2) differ, so the total is `3 + 2 + 1 + 3 = 9`.

blocks.h: Why do mirror pairs make a small state?
p: Each layer links two houses, and only the neighbours on each side matter for the next layer. With 3 colours and `a != b` there are only 6 states per layer, so the work per layer is constant.

bullets: Time: O(n) (6 states, 6 transitions each, per layer).

3429.takeaway: Go inward from both ends, keeping the best cost for each valid (left colour, right colour) pair.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Free stretches: before the first meeting, between meetings, and after the last (`n + 1` of them)
Running maximum of the gaps from the left and from the right
Largest gap on each side of a position in O(1)
How much room it needs elsewhere
The largest gap not touching meeting `i` (`gaps[0..i−1]` and `gaps[i+2..]`)
Where the meeting could be moved to
Free time created by lifting meeting `i` out: its two neighbouring gaps merge
Removing an item from a timeline
If it fits in another gap, it leaves for good and its time becomes free as well

p: `eventTime = 5`, `startTime = [1,3]`, `endTime = [2,5]`. Gaps: `[1, 1, 0]`.
The best is `2`.

blocks.h: Why is the merged gap the answer when the meeting cannot move away?
p: If the meeting cannot fit in any other gap, it must stay within the stretch formed by its two neighbouring gaps. Sliding it to one end leaves `gaps[i] + gaps[i + 1]` as one continuous free period. If it does fit elsewhere, its own duration is added to that free period.

3440.takeaway: For each meeting merge its two neighbouring gaps, and add its duration if some other gap can hold it.
